Too lazy to go over everything, so I'll go with the low hanging fruit of abiogenesis. (life forming from inorganic matter)(primordial soup etc.etc.)

It was a somewhat believable theory until we discovered how complex living organisms are. They are highly sophisticated and programmable micro-machines. I like to use a protein as an example. What are the odds of a single average length protein forming by chance? An average protein has 250 amino acids of 20 different types, so there are 20^250 combinations, which is about 10^325. How big is that number? Well, if you took every atom in the universe (10^82), turned them each into one of the 20 essential amino acids (and not the 500 others), mixed all of them together into "primordial soup", created a machine that reorganized the entire mass into random 250 long chains a trillion times a second, (never repeating!), how long would it take to get the required to get the protein we are looking for? (ignoring proper protein folding of course) Well, all matter in the universe would still decay into subatomic particles before you get it. So, if even the entire universe is unable to generate one of the basic parts, how likely is it that tens of thousands of proteins organized themselves into complex structures and micro machines, along with the dna code requjred?

This just gives you a general idea of the probability of cellular life randomly occuring complete with the dna code for reproduction. It's physically impossible, and every abiogenesis theory admits to what they call the "problem of multiplying probabilities". Even the atheist experts who determined the minimum required dna codebase of the basest lifeform, lowball the estimate at a less than 10^1000 chance of happening by chance. (I obviously think it's far more unlikely than that, but what's the point of arguing that one infinity is greater than another?)

...

The arguments against evolution are more complex, but just as valid. One is the irreducible complexity argument I'm sure you've heard. But I view it from the chains of dna code, and understand that the likelyhood of generating the irreducibly complex code through random chance. (but if someone is willing to believe that the entire code required for life can spontaneously generate, then what is a snippet of code? If 1/10^1000 is no sweat, what is 1/10^100?)

One of the simpler arguments born from testing are the mutation rates, and selection rates; showing how natural selection can't even select away the harmful mutations. (Each female would need to give birth to millions of offspring and kill all but two in order to even maintain the good dna code, let alone improve it.) Mutations are far too frequent, pretty much all are negative, and they occur far too frequently to ever be fixed through natural selection.

Time - Even if evolution worked, the time required to generate such complex dna code is not sufficient. It takes one in millions to even randomly affect two nucleotides next to each other, let alone the entire chain required for the assembly instructions for a new basic part. 14 billion years to assemble the code for even a single animal? Not even close.
